activities.anchor: Take two photographs of the same politician
activities.caption: drag the divider — one subject, two framings
activities.name: msPhotoCompare

config.prompt: Two framings of one public figure, shot on one day — drag to see what each choice builds:

before.label: the angle that towers
before.text: Shot from below, the figure fills the frame against the sky: monument status, authority, a man to be looked up at.

after.label: the blink on an inside page
after.text: Caught mid-blink, cropped small beside the text: a foolish, unguarded instant. Neither image is "just what happened" — an angle was chosen, a crop was chosen, and each choice nudges the reader.

config.why: A media product is a sequence of decisions, and decisions have makers, motives and costs.

activities.anchor: which is exactly why producers can rely on them
activities.caption: file each habit: sign system or settled convention?
activities.name: msCodeBuckets

config.prompt: Codes are the sign systems; conventions are the settled habits of a genre. File each:
config.why: Audiences learn the habits without ever naming them — which is why a cover that broke every convention would confuse rather than attract.

activities.anchor: media language works because audiences are fluent without knowing they are
activities.caption: rebuild the denotation-to-connotation read
activities.name: msCarOrder

config.prompt: The car advert, analysed in the correct order — drag the moves into place:
items: Denotation: the vehicle low and three-quarter on, wet tarmac at dusk, the city blurred, one tagline
Connotation: the low angle grants the car monument status
Connotation: the wet tarmac implies control in conditions most drivers fear
Connotation: the blurred city isolates the product as the only fixed thing in a moving world
Genre codes — the hero shot inherited from decades of car advertising — let the reader decode it all in about two seconds
config.why: First say what is literally there; then argue what it means — and support every connotation from the code itself.

activities.anchor: It is not and it does not.
activities.caption: one line of the study note overstates identification
activities.name: msListSpot

config.prompt: A student's note on how to analyse media language — one line is wrong. Click it:
lines: A radio play's language is voice, silence, music and soundscape.
A video game's language is mechanics and interface.
A list of codes earns full marks on its own — spotting them is what the exam rewards.
Each code must be tied to the meaning it constructs.
Analysis is how the code works on the audience; identification only says it is there.
config.correction: A list of codes earns nothing until each one is tied to the meaning it constructs — the reward is for analysis (how the code works on the audience), not identification (that the code is present).
config.why: Listing techniques is the subject's most common self-inflicted wound.

activities.anchor: The result is an audience that fears the wrong things
activities.caption: walk the newsroom decision
activities.name: msNewsroomBranch

config.root: Local newsroom, tonight. Two stories: a rare violent assault, and a burglary wave.

choices.label: The assault — it is what the audience will watch
choices.feedback: The overdramatisation researchers document, chosen one bulletin at a time.

choices.label: The burglary wave — statistically the bigger harm
choices.feedback: Closer to the world's actual frequencies.

drama.text: Rare violent crime gets vastly more coverage than burglary and theft, and the coverage skews further by who is accused and who is the victim. The audience's fear map ends up misdrawn.

frequency.text: Honest frequencies — but check the framing before relaxing: every act of choosing is still a construction.

construction.text: Who is shown, and who is absent? Which verb — "protesters marched" or "protesters flooded the streets"? Portrayals select, frame and repeat; that gap between the world and the news about the world is what "representations are constructions" means.

config.why: Representation analysis is structural: who is shown, in what roles, and reduced to types or not.

activities.caption: true or false — can the camera lie?
activities.name: msCameraJudge

statements.s: A camera cannot lie, so what it shows is not a construction.
statements.why: It cannot show everything — every act of choosing (angle, moment, interviewee, verb) is a construction.

statements.s: The test is not whether a portrayal is constructed — all are — but how fairly, and in whose interest.
statements.why: Construction is universal; fairness is the variable.

statements.s: Choosing the verb "marched" over "flooded the streets" is already a construction.
statements.why: Selection happens at the level of the sentence, not just the shot.

activities.anchor: Each answer explains features of the product that media language alone cannot
activities.caption: pair each industry process with its question
activities.name: msIndustryMatch

config.prompt: Three industry processes, three honest questions — pair them:

pairs.right: who funded it, and what did the funder want?
through what channels did it reach you — newsstand, cinema, broadcast schedule, platform algorithm?
how is it paid for — cover price, subscription, advertising, licence fee, in-game purchases?

config.why: The free-to-play game, the public-broadcaster drama and the tabloid front page are each explained by their answers — features that studying the text alone will never reveal.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — three funding models, three products
activities.name: msFundingCloze

config.text: A free-to-play game's energy timers come from its business model; a public broadcaster's drama comes from its %%0%%; a tabloid's type size comes from a purchase decided in %%1%%.
config.hint: One word is what the broadcaster is asked for; the other is how long a newsstand buyer hesitates.
